'''Ludwig Georg Elias Moses Bieberbach''' ({{IPA|de|ˈbiːbɐbax|lang}}; 4 December 1886 – 1 September 1982) was a German [[mathematician]], who achieved early success solving the first part of [[Hilbert's eighteenth problem]]; he is best known for formulating the [[Bieberbach conjecture]]. He was also a leading representative of [[Nazism|National Socialist]] German mathematics ("[[Deutsche Mathematik]]").<ref name="mactutor">{{MacTutor Biography|id=Bieberbach}}</ref>

==Biography==
Ludwig Bieberbach was born 4 December 1886 in [[Goddelau]], near [[Darmstadt]]. His mother, Karoline Ludwig, was the daughter of [[:de:Georg_Ludwig_(Mediziner,_1826)|Georg Ludwig]], the director of the {{ill|Heppenheim State Asylum|de|Ehemalige_Landesirrenanstalt_Heppenheim}}. His father, Eberhard Sebastian Bieberbach (1848-1893), was a physician and later director of the same asylum.<ref name="mactutor"/>

Bieberbach studied at [[University of Heidelberg|Heidelberg]] and under [[Felix Klein]] at [[University of Göttingen|Göttingen]], receiving his doctorate in 1910.<ref>{{MathGenealogy|id=19524}}</ref> His dissertation was titled ''On the theory of automorphic functions'' ({{langx|de|Theorie der automorphen Funktionen}}). He began working as a [[Privatdozent]] in 1910, at first with [[Ernst Zermelo]] at the [[University of Zurich]], and soon after with [[Arthur Moritz Schoenflies|Arthur Schoenflies]] at [[University of Königsberg|Königsberg]].

Bieberbach wrote a habilitation thesis in 1911 about [[group (mathematics)|group]]s of Euclidean motions – identifying [[Periodic Graph (Geometry)#Obtaining periodicity|conditions under which the group must have a translational subgroup whose vectors span the Euclidean space]] – that helped solve [[Hilbert's eighteenth problem|Hilbert's 18th problem]].<ref>{{cite book |author=Ben Yandell |author-link=Benjamin Yandell |title=The Honors Class: Hilbert's Problems and Their Solvers| url=https://books.google.com/books?id=3UBZDwAAQBAJ |year=2001 |publisher=CRC Press}}</ref>

Bieberbach was appointed Professor ordinarius at the [[University of Basel]] in 1913. He moved to the [[Goethe University Frankfurt|University of Frankfurt]] in 1915.
In 1916 he formulated the [[Bieberbach conjecture]], stating a necessary condition for a [[holomorphic function]] to map the open unit disc injectively into the [[complex plane]] in terms of the function's [[Taylor series]]. In 1984 [[Louis de Branges]] proved the conjecture (for this reason, the [[Bieberbach conjecture]] is sometimes called [[de Branges's theorem]]).<ref>{{cite journal |author=J. Korevaar |author-link=Jacob Korevaar |title=Ludwig Bieberbach's Conjecture and Its Proof by Louis de Branges |journal=The American Mathematical Monthly |volume=93 |number=7 |year=1986 |jstor=2323021}}</ref>

He taught at the [[Humboldt University of Berlin|University of Berlin]] from 1921&ndash;45.
He worked on [[complex analysis]] and its applications to other areas in mathematics. He is known for his work on dynamics in several complex variables, where he obtained results similar to [[Pierre Fatou|Fatou]]'s.   There is also a {{Interlanguage link multi|Bieberbach theorem|ru|3=Изодиаметрическое неравенство}} on [[space group]]s. In 1928 Bieberbach wrote a book with [[Issai Schur]] titled ''Über die Minkowskische Reduktiontheorie der positiven quadratischen Formen''.

Bieberbach was a speaker at the [[International Congress of Mathematicians]] held at Zurich in 1932.

==Politics==
Bieberbach joined the [[Sturmabteilung]] in 1933 and the [[NSDAP]] in 1937. He was enthusiastically involved in the efforts to dismiss  his Jewish colleagues, including [[Edmund Landau]] and his former coauthor [[Issai Schur]], from their posts. He also facilitated the [[Gestapo]] arrests of some close colleagues, such as [[Juliusz Schauder]]. Bieberbach was heavily influenced by [[Theodore Vahlen]], another German mathematician and anti-Semite, who along with Bieberbach founded the "[[Deutsche Mathematik]]" ("German mathematics") movement and journal of the same name. The purpose of the movement was to encourage and promote a "German" (in this case meaning [[Intuitionism|intuitionistic]]) style in mathematics. For example, Bieberbach claimed that "the [[Cauchy–Goursat theorem]] arouses intolerable displeasure" in Germans, and was representative of an abstract style of reasoning and "pronounced shrewdness" characteristic of "Jewish mathematics".<ref name="bieberbach">{{cite web|url= https://www.tabletmag.com/sections/arts-letters/articles/hitlers-math|title= Hitler's Math|date= 8 February 2017}} citing ''Deutsche Zukunft [German Future]'' of April 8, 1934 and ''{{ill|Forschungen und Fortschritte|de}} [Research and Progress]'' of June 20, 1934.</ref> Bieberbach's and Vahlen's idea of German mathematics was part of a wider trend in the scientific community in Nazi Germany towards giving the sciences racial character; there were also pseudoscientific movements for "[[Deutsche Physik]]", "[[German chemistry]]", and "[[German biology]]".

In 1945, Bieberbach was dismissed from all his academic positions because of his support of Nazism, but in 1949 was invited to lecture at the [[University of Basel]] by [[Alexander Ostrowski|Ostrowski]], who considered Bieberbach's political views irrelevant to his contributions to mathematics.<ref>{{citation|title=math.ch/100: Swiss Mathematical Society, 1910–2010|year=2010|publisher=European Mathematical Society Publishing House|location=Zürich|first=Walter|last=Gautschi|contribution=Alexander M. Ostrowski (1893–1986): His life, work, and students|pages=257–278|contribution-url=https://www.cs.purdue.edu/homes/wxg/selected_works/section_12/196.pdf}}. See in particular p.&nbsp;263: "This high esteem of scientific merits, regardless of political, personal, or other shortcomings of this attaining them, came across already in 1949, when he [Ostrowski] had the courage of inviting Bieberbach – then disgraced by his Nazi past and ostracized by the European intelligentsia – to spend a semester as guest of the university of Basel and conduct a seminar on geometric constructions."</ref>
